opus-5.5.text:
I think robotics is one of the most exciting and, at the same time, one of the most humbling areas in AI right now. We've seen tremendous progress in models that understand language, images, and even scientific structures like proteins. But the physical world is a different kind of challenge. When a model makes a mistake in text, you can regenerate the answer. When a robot makes a mistake, something falls on the floor, or worse.

What's changed recently is that we now have foundation models that bring a lot of common-sense understanding of the world: what objects are, how they're typically used, what a sensible next step looks like. Connecting that kind of semantic knowledge to low-level control is a big shift. A robot no longer has to learn from scratch that a cup is something you hold upright. That prior knowledge can come from models trained on enormous amounts of data from the web.

The bottleneck, though, is still data, specifically physical interaction data. We don't have an internet's worth of examples of robots grasping, pushing, folding, and assembling things. So a lot of the important work is figuring out how to get more out of the data we have: learning from human videos, using simulation well, sharing data across different robot bodies, and building systems that can improve from their own experience.

So my assessment is optimistic but measured. I expect steady and, at times, surprising progress in narrower settings, such as warehouses, labs, and structured environments. In science, for instance, robotic automation combined with AI could close the loop between hypothesis and experiment, which I find very compelling. The general-purpose household robot that reliably handles the messiness of everyday life is a harder problem. It will take longer than the most enthusiastic predictions suggest. But the trajectory has clearly changed, and I think the next few years will be very interesting.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes near-term progress in narrower, structured settings from the longer timeline for reliable general-purpose household robots.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm actually quite optimistic about robotics, but I think it's worth being precise about why, because the optimism rests on something that's changed fairly recently.

For a long time, the bottleneck in robotics wasn't really the hardware. The hardware was clunky and expensive, yes, but the deeper problem was that we didn't know how to give a robot a general understanding of the world. Every task had to be hand-engineered. You'd spend months getting a robot to pick up a particular object in a particular lighting condition, and then you'd move the table six inches and it would fall apart. That brittleness was the core issue.

What's shifted is that large models trained on language and vision have given us something that looks a lot like common sense about the physical world. A model that has absorbed enormous amounts of text and images already knows that cups hold liquids, that you grasp a mug by the handle, that a kitchen has a certain layout. When you connect that kind of representation to a robot's actuators, you suddenly get systems that can generalize to situations they've never explicitly been trained on. That's genuinely new, and it's why you're seeing this surge of interest.

Now, I'd temper that with a few things. The first is data. Language models got to where they are because the internet handed us trillions of tokens for free. There's no equivalent for robot actions. You can't scrape the web for examples of how to fold a towel with a particular gripper. So the field is working on how to get that data, whether through simulation, through teleoperation, through learning from human video, and I think the answer will be some combination of all of them. But it's a real constraint, and it means progress will be gated by how clever we are about it.

The second is that the physical world is unforgiving in ways that language isn't. If a language model makes a mistake, you get a wrong sentence. If a robot makes a mistake, it may break something or hurt someone. So the reliability bar is much higher, and reliability is exactly where learned systems have historically struggled. Getting from a demo that works eighty percent of the time to a product that works ninety-nine point nine percent of the time is where most of the hard engineering lives.

And the third is that I think people underestimate how much of robotics is still a systems problem. Perception, planning, control, hardware, safety, all of these have to come together, and a breakthrough in one doesn't automatically unlock the others.

So my honest assessment is that we're at the beginning of a real inflection point, not the end of one. Over the next few years I expect we'll see robots in structured environments, warehouses, labs, certain kinds of manufacturing, become much more capable and much more general than they are today. The fully general household robot that people imagine is further out, because homes are the hardest environment there is. But the trajectory has changed, and that's what makes me optimistic. The question is no longer whether learning-based approaches can work for robotics. It's how fast we can scale them responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes near-term prospects—more capable robots in structured settings over the next few years—from the longer-term prospect of general household robots.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic about robotics, but there’s a substantial gap between having a system that can reason about a task and having one that can reliably carry it out in the physical world. A robot has to perceive its surroundings, understand what might happen when it acts, and adapt when things don’t go as expected.

The exciting prospect is bringing those capabilities together. Learning can help robots acquire skills that are difficult to program explicitly, while planning can help them use those skills in new situations. But reliability matters enormously: a successful demonstration is only a beginning. We need systems that can handle variation, recognize their limitations, and operate safely around people. So I see tremendous potential, alongside some very challenging work ahead.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses optimism alongside major challenges, but does not make the robotics outlook depend on the time horizon being considered.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m very optimistic about robotics, though there are still some very hard problems to solve. The physical world is much less forgiving than a digital environment. A robot has to perceive what’s happening, understand what its actions might do, and respond safely when something unexpected happens.

One of the exciting prospects is that we can bring together advances in perception, language, and learning to build systems that generalize beyond a single task. But there’s a significant gap between an impressive demonstration and a robot that works reliably in someone’s home. For me, the key question is how we close that gap—how we make these systems useful, adaptable, and trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response describes optimism alongside current challenges, but does not frame robotics’ prospects as differing by time horizon.
